questions.title: Anatomical relation of lumbar to cervical vertebrae (inferior)
questions.question: What is the correct anatomical term that describes the relationship of the lumbar vertebrae to the cervical vertebrae?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Medial describes distance from the midline in the coronal plane, a different axis from the head-to-foot position being asked about here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lateral, like medial, describes the mediolateral axis, not the craniocaudal (head-to-foot) axis that relates the lumbar and cervical vertebrae to each other.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Posterior describes the anteroposterior (front-to-back) axis, a third axis unrelated to the vertebral column's head-to-foot ordering.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Superior would describe the lumbar vertebrae as closer to the head than the cervical vertebrae, the opposite of their actual relationship.
explanations.E: Correct. Superior and inferior describe position along the body's craniocaudal axis: the cervical vertebrae (C1-C7) form the most superior spinal segment, immediately below the skull, while the lumbar vertebrae (L1-L5) lie inferior to the thoracic vertebrae and superior only to the sacrum and coccyx. Relative to the cervical vertebrae, then, the lumbar vertebrae are inferior -- closer to the feet along the vertebral column's own craniocaudal sequence. This is a pure application of the standard anatomical-position vocabulary, independent of the medial/lateral and anterior/posterior axes offered as distractors.

questions.learning_objective: Anatomical relation of lumbar to cervical vertebrae (inferior)

questions.title: Muscle role that prevents unwanted movement at intermediate joints (synergist)
questions.question: Which term of the followings describes the muscles that contract to prevent the unwanted movements at the intermediate joints?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The prime mover (agonist) is the muscle that initiates and maintains the movement itself, not the muscle that cancels unwanted side-effects at other joints it crosses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Agonist is another name for the prime mover, the muscle producing the movement, not the one preventing unwanted movement elsewhere.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The antagonist opposes the prime mover's own action at the joint being moved; it does not specifically address unwanted movement at intermediate joints the prime mover crosses.
explanations.D: Correct. The synergist contracts to cancel out unwanted movements that the prime mover would otherwise produce at other, intermediate joints it crosses on its way to the joint that matters, so that the prime mover's action there becomes maximal. A classic example is the wrist extensors acting as synergists during finger flexion, preventing the long flexor tendons from also flexing the wrist as they cross it. This is distinct from the fixator, which stabilises the prime mover's own origin rather than an intermediate joint.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The fixator (stabiliser) fixes the origin of the prime mover, or stabilises the joint the prime mover acts on, so its pull has something to work against -- a related but distinct job from the synergist's role at intermediate joints.

questions.learning_objective: Muscle role that prevents unwanted movement at intermediate joints (synergist)

questions.title: Structures that are eight in number (carpal bones)
questions.question: Which of the followings are eight (8) in number?

explanations.A: Correct. The carpus (wrist) is built of eight carpal bones in two rows of four: proximally the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform, and distally the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate. A hand skeleton listed with only seven bones in this group is short one -- the commonest distractor against the correct count of eight. This count is fixed and does not vary the way, for example, the number of ribs or vertebral segments can show minor normal variation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There are five metatarsal bones, one for each digit of the foot, not eight.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There are seven tarsal bones (talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, three cuneiforms), not eight.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There are seven cervical vertebrae (C1-C7), a number many students confuse with the eight carpal bones precisely because both are commonly tested landmark counts.
explanations.E: Incorrect. There are five sacral vertebrae before they fuse into the single sacrum, not eight.

questions.learning_objective: Structures that are eight in number (carpal bones)

questions.title: Fibrocartilaginous lip that deepens a joint socket (labrum)
questions.question: Which of the followings describes the fibrocartilaginous lip that extends from the edge of a joint socket to deepen it?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An intracapsular ligament is a ligament lying within the joint capsule (such as the cruciate ligaments of the knee), not a rim of fibrocartilage deepening a socket.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A tendon sheath is a synovial-lined tube that reduces friction on a tendon running past a joint; it plays no role in deepening a bony socket.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A meniscus is a wedge of fibrocartilage that improves congruity between two nearly flat articulating surfaces (as at the knee), a different job from deepening a socket for a ball-shaped bone.
explanations.D: Correct. A labrum (Latin 'lip') is a ring of fibrocartilage attached to the bony margin of a shallow joint socket, extending it to increase both the depth of the socket and the contact area with the opposing convex bone. The two named examples are the glenoid labrum of the shoulder and the acetabular labrum of the hip, the two joints whose bony sockets are shallowest relative to the ball they receive. This improves stability while preserving the joint's mobility, unlike a meniscus, ligament, tendon sheath or bursa, none of which deepens a socket.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A bursa is a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between a tendon or muscle and adjacent bone or skin; it does not deepen a joint socket.

questions.learning_objective: Fibrocartilaginous lip that deepens a joint socket (labrum)

questions.title: Correct statement about blood vessels (splenic sinusoids)
questions.question: As regard blood vessels, which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Veins of the lower limb have no valves
options.C: Blockage of anastomotic arteries causes severe tissue damage
options.D: Pulmonary vein is interposed between two capillary beds
options.E: Blood sinusoids are numerous in the spleen

explanations.A: Incorrect. Veins of the lower limb are richly supplied with valves, precisely because they must resist gravity to return blood to the heart; the opposite statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Venae comitantes (paired veins) typically accompany small- and medium-sized arteries, not veins in isolation, running alongside the artery within a shared fascial sheath.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Blockage of an anastomotic artery is characteristically well tolerated because the anastomosis provides an alternative route for blood flow, unlike blockage of an end-artery, which does cause severe tissue damage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood directly from the lung capillaries to the left atrium, with no second, intervening capillary bed -- that two-bed-in-series arrangement is instead the defining feature of a portal circulation.
explanations.E: Correct. Blood sinusoids are a wide-bore, discontinuous- or fenestrated-endothelium capillary type that allows free passage of larger particles and even whole blood cells, unlike an ordinary continuous capillary. They are numerous specifically in organs that need this free exchange -- the spleen (where red-pulp sinusoids let macrophages test red-cell deformability and remove aged cells), the liver and the bone marrow -- and their width also makes them a low-pressure blood reservoir.

questions.learning_objective: Correct statement about blood vessels (splenic sinusoids)

questions.title: Enlarged lymph node group after a breast abscess (axillary)
questions.question: A 31-year-old female patient had a breast abscess. A few days later, the lymph nodes in her armpit were enlarged. Which one of these groups of lymph nodes was affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cervical lymph nodes drain the head and neck, not the breast, and are not located in the armpit.
explanations.B: Correct. Approximately 75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary lymph nodes, especially the pectoral group, which is precisely why an infective or malignant breast process classically presents with palpable, enlarged nodes in the armpit. This makes the axillary group the first and most important site to examine clinically whenever a breast pathology, infective or neoplastic, is suspected.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inguinal lymph nodes drain the lower limb, perineum and lower anal canal, not the breast, and lie in the groin rather than the armpit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The supraclavicular nodes (Virchow's node on the left being classically linked to abdominal malignancy) lie above the clavicle, not in the armpit, and are not the primary drainage site for the breast.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The mediastinal lymph nodes lie within the thoracic cavity and drain thoracic viscera; they are not palpable in the armpit and are not the breast's chief lymphatic drainage.

questions.learning_objective: Enlarged lymph node group after a breast abscess (axillary)

questions.title: Cranial nerve carrying parasympathetic fibres (facial, VII)
questions.question: Which of the following cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibers?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplying only superior oblique; it carries no parasympathetic fibres.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The trigeminal nerve is chiefly sensory, with a separate motor root to the muscles of mastication only; the parasympathetic fibres that travel alongside some of its branches actually originate from cranial nerve VII and merely share part of its course.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The abducent nerve is purely motor, supplying only lateral rectus; it carries no parasympathetic fibres.
explanations.D: Correct. Of the twelve cranial nerves, only four carry parasympathetic fibres: III, VII, IX and X. The facial nerve's parasympathetic fibres arise from the superior salivatory and lacrimal nuclei and travel via the nervus intermedius before synapsing in the pterygopalatine or submandibular ganglion, ultimately supplying the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands and the mucosa of the nose and palate.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The vestibulocochlear nerve is purely sensory, carrying hearing and balance information; it carries no parasympathetic fibres.

questions.learning_objective: Cranial nerve carrying parasympathetic fibres (facial, VII)

questions.title: Structure that contributes to placenta formation (chorion)
questions.question: Which one of the following contributes to the formation of the placenta?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The amnion is a separate, thin, avascular membrane that forms the fluid-filled sac around the embryo; it takes no part in placenta formation.
explanations.B: Correct. The placenta forms from two contributions that fuse at the implantation site: a fetal part, the chorion frondosum (villous chorion), built from trophoblast plus the extraembryonic mesoderm lining it, and a maternal part, the decidua basalis, from the underlying endometrium. Of the five structures listed, only the chorion is a direct structural component of the placental disc itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The yolk sac contributes to the primitive gut (via its endodermal lining, incorporated during folding) and to the origin of primordial germ cells; it contributes nothing to the placenta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The allantois contributes to the urachus and, via its vessels, to the umbilical arteries and vein, but it is not itself a structural component of the placental disc.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The hypoblast is an early bilaminar-disc layer that gives rise to the yolk sac lining, one step further removed from placenta formation still.

questions.learning_objective: Structure that contributes to placenta formation (chorion)

questions.title: Origin of the primitive gut (yolk sac)
questions.question: The primitive gut is developed from which one of the followings?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The connecting stalk becomes the umbilical cord's connective-tissue core, not the gut.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The chorion frondosum contributes to the placenta, not to the gut tube.
explanations.C: Correct. Following lateral and cephalocaudal folding of the trilaminar embryonic disc in the fourth week, part of the endoderm-lined yolk sac cavity is incorporated into the body of the embryo as a continuous tube: the primitive gut. The primitive gut divides into foregut, midgut and hindgut, each retaining the endodermal lining derived from the yolk sac and going on to form the epithelial lining and glandular derivatives of the alimentary tract, while surrounding splanchnic mesoderm supplies the muscular and connective-tissue coats.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The allantois contributes to the urachus and umbilical vessels, not to the gut tube itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The amnion forms the fluid-filled amniotic sac around the embryo; it does not form the gut.

questions.learning_objective: Origin of the primitive gut (yolk sac)

questions.title: Characteristic feature of placenta accreta (villous invasion of myometrium)
questions.question: Placenta accreta is characterized by which one of the followings?

options.A: Separation of the placenta from the uterine wall
options.B: Invasion of chorionic villi into the myometrium
options.D: Placenta is empty in the middle
options.E: Presents in the lower segment of the uterus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Premature separation of an otherwise normally attached placenta from the uterine wall describes placental abruption, a different condition from accreta.
explanations.B: Correct. Placenta accreta is an abnormality of placental attachment in which chorionic villi attach directly to, or invade into, the myometrium, because the decidua basalis is deficient or absent at the implantation site, rather than remaining confined to a normal decidual plane. This depth-of-invasion abnormality is why the placenta cannot separate normally at delivery, carrying a high risk of massive postpartum haemorrhage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Placenta accreta is not defined by placental size; abnormal size is a separate finding (as in a small placenta from placental insufficiency) unrelated to the depth of villous invasion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A placenta 'empty in the middle' describes placenta fenestrata (a central defect), a structural variant distinct from accreta's abnormal depth of invasion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Presenting in the lower uterine segment, over or near the internal os, describes placenta praevia, a positional abnormality distinct from accreta, though the two conditions can coexist.

questions.learning_objective: Characteristic feature of placenta accreta (villous invasion of myometrium)

questions.title: When ovum maturation is completed (fertilization)
questions.question: The completion of ovum maturation occurs after which one of the followings?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Birth occurs long before ovum maturation is completed; primary oocytes remain arrested in meiotic prophase from before birth until much later.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cleavage (the early mitotic divisions of the zygote) happens after fertilization has already triggered completion of meiosis II, so it follows rather than causes ovum maturation.
explanations.C: Correct. Oogenesis arrests twice. The primary oocyte stays arrested in prophase of meiosis I until ovulation, when the LH surge triggers completion of meiosis I, producing a secondary oocyte that immediately arrests again, this time in metaphase II. It is this secondary oocyte, not a mature ovum, that is ovulated and penetrated by a sperm; meiosis II, and so true ovum maturation, is completed only if and when fertilization actually occurs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ovulation releases the secondary oocyte still arrested in metaphase II, not a mature ovum -- true maturation is completed only afterward, at fertilization.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Puberty marks the resumption of cyclical ovulation, not the completion of any individual oocyte's maturation.

questions.learning_objective: When ovum maturation is completed (fertilization)

questions.title: Week the primitive node appears (third week)
questions.question: The primitive node appears in the embryonic disc at which week of the followings?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Week 1 is occupied by fertilization, cleavage and blastocyst formation; gastrulation, which forms the primitive node, has not yet begun.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Week 2 ('the week of twos') produces the bilaminar germ disc, the amniotic cavity and the primary yolk sac -- still before gastrulation and the primitive node appear.
explanations.C: Correct. Gastrulation begins early in the third week (around day 15-16), forming the primitive streak at the caudal end of the bilaminar disc and the primitive node at its cranial end, and converting the disc into a trilaminar disc with three germ layers. This places the primitive node's appearance squarely in week 3, after the one-layer week 1 and two-layer week 2, and before the folding of week 4.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Week 4 is when folding of the flat trilaminar disc into a three-dimensional body occurs, after the primitive node has already appeared and done its organising work in week 3.
explanations.E: Incorrect. By week 5, early organogenesis is already underway, well after the primitive node appeared in week 3.

questions.learning_objective: Week the primitive node appears (third week)

questions.title: Source of human chorionic gonadotrophin (syncytiotrophoblast)
questions.question: The human chorionic gonadotrophin hormone is released from which one of the followings?

explanations.A: Correct. Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) is a glycoprotein hormone secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast, the outer, multinucleated, invasive layer of the trophoblast that lies in direct contact with maternal blood once lacunae form within it. hCG maintains the corpus luteum's progesterone output through the early weeks of pregnancy, before the placenta itself takes over, and is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fetal endothelial cells form the walls of the fetal vessels within the chorionic villi; they are a vascular, not an endocrine, component and do not secrete hCG.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cytotrophoblast is the inner, mononuclear, mitotically active layer that generates new cells which fuse into the syncytiotrophoblast; it does not itself secrete hCG.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extraembryonic mesoderm forms the connective-tissue core of a secondary chorionic villus; it has no comparable endocrine, hCG-secreting role.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Decidua basalis is the maternal contribution to the placenta, formed from the endometrium; it is not fetal trophoblast tissue and does not secrete hCG.

questions.learning_objective: Source of human chorionic gonadotrophin (syncytiotrophoblast)

questions.title: Character of the outer nuclear membrane (continuous with RER)
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of the outer nuclear membrane?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with rough, not smooth, endoplasmic reticulum -- both surfaces specifically carry bound ribosomes, a feature rough ER has and smooth ER lacks.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chromatin granules lie within the nucleus, associated with the inner nuclear membrane and the nuclear lamina, not scattered on the outer nuclear membrane's own surface.
explanations.C: Correct. The outer nuclear membrane is directly continuous with the membrane of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and both are studded on their cytoplasm-facing surface with bound ribosomes for the same reason -- rER is, structurally, an extension of the nucleus's own outer membrane out into the cytoplasm. This continuity is why polyribosomes are seen on the outer nuclear envelope as well as on the rER proper.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acidophilia (staining pink/eosinophilic) is a property of protein-poor, lipid- or mitochondria-rich cytoplasm; the ribosome-studded outer nuclear membrane instead contributes to basophilia, not acidophilia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The nuclear envelope, including the region around the outer membrane, is perforated by numerous nuclear pores that regulate traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm; it is not pore-free.

questions.learning_objective: Character of the outer nuclear membrane (continuous with RER)

questions.title: True statement about chromatin (euchromatin is active)
questions.question: Which of the following is true concerning chromatin?

options.D: It is attached to the outer nuclear membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chromatin is basophilic, not acidophilic, because of the acidic phosphate groups of its nucleic acid.
explanations.B: Correct. Chromatin exists in two forms: euchromatin, the extended, uncoiled form that is transcriptionally active, predominating in metabolically active cells and giving a pale, vesicular nucleus; and heterochromatin, the coiled, condensed, inactive form, predominating in quiescent cells such as the small lymphocyte and giving a dense, dark nucleus. Because euchromatin is loosely packed, RNA polymerase and transcription factors can access its DNA freely, which is exactly what makes it the transcriptionally active form. A cell that is very metabolically active, synthesising large amounts of protein, therefore has a nucleus that looks pale and vesicular under the microscope, dominated by euchromatin rather than the dense, dark heterochromatin of a quiescent cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heterochromatin is the condensed, transcriptionally inactive form of chromatin -- the opposite of the correct statement about euchromatin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chromatin is associated with the inner nuclear membrane and nuclear lamina, not the outer nuclear membrane, which instead carries ribosomes and is continuous with rough ER.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chromatin is DNA complexed with histone and non-histone proteins, not a lipid.

questions.learning_objective: True statement about chromatin (euchromatin is active)

questions.title: Non-membranous organelles (microfilaments)
questions.question: Which of the following are non-membranous organelles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitochondria are bounded by a double membrane (outer and inner, the inner folded into cristae); they are a membranous organelle.
explanations.B: Correct. Organelles are classified by whether they have a limiting membrane. The membranous organelles are the plasma membrane, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes; the non-membranous organelles are the ribosomes and the cytoskeleton -- microfilaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments -- together with the centrioles, cilia and flagella the microtubules build. Microfilaments are therefore correctly classed as non-membranous.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glycogen is a cell inclusion (a non-living, temporary store of material), not an organelle of any kind, membranous or otherwise.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysosomes are bounded by a single limiting membrane; they are a membranous organelle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Crystals, like glycogen, are a cell inclusion rather than an organelle, and so fall outside the membranous/non-membranous organelle classification altogether.

questions.learning_objective: Non-membranous organelles (microfilaments)

questions.title: Epithelium type forming the epidermis (keratinized stratified squamous)
questions.question: What type of epithelium forms the epidermis of skin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of flattened cells, far too thin to protect an exposed body surface from abrasion; it lines structures such as blood vessels and alveoli instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells, typically an absorptive or secretory lining (such as the gut), not a multilayered protective covering like skin.
explanations.C: Correct. The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium: many cell layers thick, flattened at the surface, and 'keratinized' because those surface cells lose their nuclei and organelles and fill with the tough, water-resistant protein keratin, forming a dead, protective outer layer that is continuously shed and replaced from below. This keratinized surface is what distinguishes it from non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which lines moist internal surfaces such as the oesophagus, vagina and cornea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium shares the many-layered, flattened-surface structure but its surface cells stay alive and nucleated; it lines moist internal surfaces (oesophagus, vagina, cornea), not the exposed, keratinizing surface of the skin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is a single true layer of cells of varying height that appears multilayered; it lines structures such as the trachea, not the skin.

questions.learning_objective: Epithelium type forming the epidermis (keratinized stratified squamous)

questions.title: What a Barr body is (inactive X chromosome)
questions.question: What is Barr body?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Barr body is specifically the inactivated, not the active, X chromosome -- the opposite of this statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Y chromosome is never inactivated to form a Barr body; X-inactivation is a phenomenon specific to the X chromosome.
explanations.C: Correct. The Barr body (sex chromatin) is one X chromosome, inactivated and condensed into heterochromatin, seen as a dark plaque against the inner nuclear membrane. Because exactly one X stays active in every cell regardless of total X count, the Barr body count always equals the number of X chromosomes minus one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Y chromosome is not inactivated at all under normal circumstances, active or otherwise, and does not form a Barr body.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An autosome is any non-sex chromosome; the Barr body phenomenon is specific to the X chromosome, a sex chromosome, not an autosome.

questions.title: True feature of ribosomes (formed of 2 subunits)
questions.question: Which of the following features is true concerning ribosomes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes attach to rough endoplasmic reticulum (and to the outer nuclear membrane), not to the Golgi apparatus, which instead receives already-synthesised protein by transport vesicle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomes attach to rough, not smooth, endoplasmic reticulum -- smooth ER is defined precisely by the absence of bound ribosomes on its surface.
explanations.C: Correct. A ribosome is a non-membranous particle of ribosomal RNA and protein, assembled in the nucleolus as a large and a small subunit of unequal size; the two subunits return to the cytoplasm separately and join one another, held together by threading messenger RNA, only during active protein synthesis. The growing polypeptide chain is carried on the large subunit as translation proceeds along the mRNA. Ribosomes linked together along one strand of mRNA form polyribosomes (polysomes), seen on electron microscopy as bead-like rosettes or spiral chains.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribosomes are basophilic, not acidophilic, because of the acidic phosphate groups of their ribosomal RNA -- this basophilia is exactly what makes protein-secreting cells such as the plasma cell stain deeply basophilic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A ribosome has no membrane at all, let alone a double one; it is one of only two classes of non-membranous organelle, alongside the cytoskeleton.

questions.learning_objective: True feature of ribosomes (formed of 2 subunits)

questions.title: Substance secreted by mast cells (histamine)
questions.question: Which of the following is secreted by mast cells?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ground substance (matrix) is secreted generally by connective-tissue cells such as the fibroblast, not specifically identified with the mast cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Steroid hormones are secreted by cells such as those of the adrenal cortex and gonads, not by the mast cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Antibodies are secreted by the plasma cell, a different connective-tissue cell derived from the B lymphocyte, not by the mast cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Collagen fibres are secreted by the fibroblast, not by the mast cell.
explanations.E: Correct. The mast cell's cytoplasm is packed with metachromatic secretory granules that, on stimulation -- classically by IgE cross-linking in a type I hypersensitivity reaction -- degranulate to release histamine (raising vascular permeability, contracting smooth muscle, causing itching) and heparin (an anticoagulant), along with other mediators such as leukotrienes. The mast cell is derived from a bone-marrow progenitor distinct from the basophil, despite the two cells' similar function and appearance. This degranulation reaction underlies immediate (type I) hypersensitivity, ranging from localised urticaria and allergic rhinitis to systemic anaphylaxis at its most severe.

questions.title: True statement about membranous organelles (Golgi is the secretory apparatus)
questions.question: Which of the following is true concerning membranous organelles?

options.A: Lysosomes are concerned with protein synthesis
options.B: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum is the digestive apparatus of the cell
options.C: Golgi is the secretory apparatus of the cell
options.D: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum is the powerhouse of the cell
options.E: Mitochondria are concerned with lipid synthesis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lysosomes digest material (via their acid hydrolase enzymes); protein synthesis is instead the role of ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum is the site of protein synthesis and segregation, one step upstream of the Golgi; digestion is the role of lysosomes, not rER.
explanations.C: Correct. Among the cell's membranous organelles, the Golgi apparatus is specifically the one responsible for the final modification, concentration, packaging and dispatch of secretory products -- receiving newly synthesised protein from rough ER at its cis face, modifying it through its stacked cisternae, and budding off finished secretory vesicles or primary lysosomes from its trans face -- which is why it is described as the secretory apparatus of the cell. This places the Golgi one step downstream of rough endoplasmic reticulum, which synthesises and segregates the protein but does not itself modify or package it for export. A transfer vesicle arriving at the Golgi's cis face is therefore Golgi input, not Golgi product -- the products, secretory vesicles and primary lysosomes, leave only from the trans face.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is chiefly concerned with lipid/steroid synthesis and drug detoxification, not energy production; the mitochondrion, not smooth ER, is the cell's powerhouse.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Mitochondria are chiefly concerned with generating ATP through oxidative phosphorylation, not lipid synthesis, which is instead a smooth endoplasmic reticulum function.

questions.learning_objective: True statement about membranous organelles (Golgi is the secretory apparatus)

questions.title: Organ with reticular connective tissue (spleen)
questions.question: Which one of the following has reticular connective tissue?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stomach wall is built of mucosa, submucosa and muscular layers with ordinary loose/dense connective tissue, not a reticular-tissue stroma.
explanations.B: Correct. Reticular connective tissue is a delicate type in which reticular cells and fine, silver-stainable type III collagen (reticular) fibres form a supporting meshwork rather than a free-standing tissue of their own. It forms the stroma -- the supporting framework around the functional cells -- of the spleen, along with the lymph node and liver.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The heart's connective-tissue framework (the cardiac skeleton, and the endomysium around individual myocytes) is not classed as reticular connective tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cartilage is its own distinct connective-tissue type (hyaline, elastic or fibrocartilage), built around chondrocytes in a firm matrix, not reticular tissue.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tendon is dense regular connective tissue, made of parallel type I collagen bundles for tensile strength, not reticular connective tissue.

questions.learning_objective: Organ with reticular connective tissue (spleen)

questions.title: Epithelium type in taste buds (neuroepithelium)
questions.question: Which of the following is the type of epithelium present in taste buds?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Surface (covering/lining) epithelium is one of the four classes of epithelium, but it describes a general lining role, not the sensory-receptor specialisation the taste bud actually has.
explanations.B: Correct. Neuro-epithelium is one of the four classes of epithelial tissue (alongside surface, glandular and myo-epithelium): epithelial cells modified to act as sensory receptors, receiving the stimulus for a sensation. The taste bud of the tongue is the standard example, its receptor cells detecting the chemical stimulus of taste.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glandular epithelium is specialised for secretion, not for sensory reception; it describes the epithelium of glands, not the taste bud's receptor cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myoepithelium is epithelium modified with contractile properties (as around secretory acini and ducts of glands), a different specialisation from the taste bud's sensory role.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 'Simple epithelium' describes a single-layer arrangement by structure, not the functional, sensory-receptor specialisation of neuro-epithelium that the taste bud actually shows.
